cases.abstract: A larger context window does not necessarily mean that a language model can use evidence wherever it appears. We diagnose this gap through controlled multi-document question answering and synthetic key-value retrieval, varying context length and the position of the single relevant item without changing the required answer. Across the evaluated question-answering models, accuracy is generally highest when evidence appears near the beginning or end and lower in the middle; some configurations perform worse than answering without documents. Extended-context versions behave almost identically to their shorter-context counterparts when both can accommodate the input. Repeating the query before and after the context largely resolves synthetic retrieval failures but does not remove the positional pattern in question answering, distinguishing successful exact lookup from effective evidence use. Encoder-decoder models are relatively insensitive to position within their training-time context lengths but develop middle-context degradation on longer inputs. In a standard retrieval pipeline, reader accuracy also saturates before retrieval recall. Together, these findings show why accepted context length and retrieval recall alone are insufficient indicators of downstream question-answering performance.
cases.methods: The diagnostic design holds the answer fixed while moving its supporting evidence. For 2,655 NaturalQuestions-Open queries with paragraph answers, each prompt contains one annotated answer passage and distractors retrieved for relevance but filtered to exclude annotated answers. Reordering the answer passage across contexts of 10, 20, or 30 documents tests position sensitivity; varying the distractor count tests the burden of additional context. Closed-book prompts and an oracle prompt containing only the answer passage provide reference points for memory-based answering and evidence use without distraction. A complementary lookup task replaces language passages with unique random UUID key-value pairs, reducing semantic confounds while preserving the need to access a designated item. The experiments use greedy decoding and score whether the correct answer or value appears in the output. Repeating the query around the context then tests whether query-aware contextualization affects lookup and question answering differently.
cases.results: The effect of query placement is sharply task-dependent. With 300 UUID key-value pairs, GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) reaches 100% accuracy when the query appears both before and after the data, whereas its worst-position accuracy without this arrangement is 45.6%. Yet the same intervention leaves the question-answering position pattern largely unchanged, slightly helping evidence at the beginning while slightly hurting other positions. The lookup result therefore does not establish a general remedy for reasoning over retrieved text. The Claude-1.3 variants' near-perfect synthetic retrieval also coexists with position-sensitive question answering. On the latter task, some GPT-3.5-Turbo configurations with 20 or 30 documents fall below the 56.1% closed-book reference, despite including an answer passage. Adding evidence can thus be counterproductive when it is difficult to access among distractors. In the standard retrieval pipeline, additional documents beyond 20 yield only marginal reader gains while recall continues to improve, making effective evidence use, rather than context capacity alone, a consequential bottleneck.
cases.notes: Emphasized a diagnostic contribution, not a proposed fix. Query repetition repairs exact UUID lookup but not multi-document QA. Architecture-related explanations remain hypotheses. The stated QA decline exceeding 20% was omitted because its scale is unclear. Retrieved distractors exclude annotated answers rather than all plausible answers; the unambiguous-question check reportedly preserved the trends.

cases.abstract: Retrieval can supply relevant text without ensuring that a generated claim is supported by it. SELF-RAG addresses this distinction by teaching a language model to decide when to retrieve and to evaluate passage relevance, evidential support, and response utility through dedicated reflection tokens. A critic trained on GPT-4 feedback annotates instruction-output data offline; the generator then learns text and reflection tokens with a standard next-token objective. During inference, sentence-level candidate continuations are ranked using generation probabilities and weighted self-evaluations, allowing retrieval frequency and evidential emphasis to be adjusted without retraining. Llama 2 models with 7B and 13B parameters are evaluated zero-shot on six tasks spanning factual questions, closed-set decisions, biographies, and cited long-form answers. On ASQA, the 7B model obtains 66.9% citation precision versus 5.0% for a model trained on the same instruction-output pairs with retrieval added only at inference, using the same five supplied documents. These gains do not imply improvement on every measure: ASQA str-em correctness remains below that baseline, and increasing the support weight improves citation precision while reducing MAUVE, the fluency metric.
cases.methods: SELF-RAG turns evidence checking into a learned part of generation rather than a separate test-time critic call. A Llama 2 critic, trained on GPT-4 reflection labels, first decides whether each training segment needs retrieval. Retrieved passages receive relevance labels, and relevant passages are paired with judgments of support for the target segment; a utility label assesses the response independently of those passages. The generator learns to predict ordinary text and reflection tokens from these augmented examples, while retrieved passage tokens are excluded from the loss. At inference, the generator produces its own evaluations. For each retrieved passage, it generates a candidate sentence and scores the continuation using its generation probability plus weighted, normalized probabilities of favorable critique tokens. Segment-level beam search retains promising continuations. This makes evidential support part of output selection while allowing its importance, or retrieval frequency, to be adjusted without another training run.
cases.results: With the same five supplied ASQA passages, SELF-RAG 7B raises citation precision from 5.0% to 66.9% and recall from 7.5% to 67.8% relative to Llama2-FT 7B, trained on the same instruction-output pairs but augmented with retrieval only at inference. Better attribution does not translate into uniformly better answering: str-em correctness is 30.0 versus 31.0. This distinction matters because evidence support and answer content are separate evaluation targets. A smaller-budget ablation reinforces the role of reflective training: with 50,000 training examples and 150 sampled ASQA questions, replacing it with training on the top retrieved passage without reflection tokens lowers str-em from 32.1 to 18.1. That comparison supports the training configuration rather than isolating any single token's effect. At inference, increasing the support weight improves citation precision but reduces MAUVE. Raising the retrieval threshold reduces retrieval frequency, with greater accuracy deterioration on PopQA than PubHealth, indicating that the appropriate amount of retrieval depends on the task.
cases.notes: Used task-specific table entries rather than the broad superiority language in the body: SELF-RAG does not lead every ASQA correctness metric. Main models use 150,000 instruction-output pairs; ablations use 50,000, with ASQA ablations restricted to 150 sampled instances. The no-critic variant also changes passage handling, so its difference is not attributed solely to a reflection token. MAUVE is retained as the reported fluency metric; increased citation precision is not treated as complete evidential support.
